questions.q: Which group contains only DNA viruses?
o: Influenza virus, measles virus and poliovirus
Rabies virus, mumps virus and HIV
Tobacco mosaic virus, rotavirus and dengue virus
questions.x: Herpes-, adeno- and poxviruses all have double-stranded DNA. Every virus in the other groups has RNA as its genetic material.

questions.q: Most viruses have a size in the range of about:
questions.x: Viruses are roughly 20–300 nm across, far smaller than bacteria (about 1–10 µm). This is why most can only be seen with an electron microscope.

questions.q: HIV shows a very high rate of mutation mainly because its reverse transcriptase:
o: Is produced by the host's B cells
Works only in the presence of antibiotics
Makes many errors and does not correct them while copying RNA into DNA
questions.x: Reverse transcriptase lacks proofreading, so many mistakes enter each new copy of the genome. This produces many variants of HIV within one person.

questions.q: In aerobic bacteria, which have no mitochondria, the electron transport chain is located in the:
questions.x: Prokaryotes carry their respiratory electron carriers and ATP synthase in the cell (plasma) membrane, which does the job of the inner mitochondrial membrane.

questions.q: Pyruvate, the end product of glycolysis, contains how many carbon atoms?
questions.x: Pyruvate (pyruvic acid) is a three-carbon compound; one glucose (6C) gives two pyruvate. The two-carbon unit is the acetyl group formed later in the link reaction.

questions.q: A monoacylglycerol is formed when glycerol is joined to:
questions.x: 'Mono' means one: a monoacylglycerol has a single fatty acid (acyl group) esterified to glycerol. Two fatty acids give a diacylglycerol and three a triacylglycerol (triglyceride).

questions.q: Why can adenine not form a stable base pair with cytosine in the double helix?
o: Their hydrogen-bonding groups do not match; only thymine matches adenine
Cytosine is a purine and too large to fit
Cytosine is found only in RNA
Adenine and cytosine carry the same charge
questions.x: Base pairing depends on matching hydrogen-bonding groups: adenine matches thymine, and guanine matches cytosine. Cytosine is a pyrimidine present in both DNA and RNA.

questions.q: Water, carbon dioxide and mineral salts in a cell are classed as:
questions.x: These are small compounds without a carbon–hydrogen skeleton, so they are inorganic. Organic compounds such as carbohydrates and proteins are built on carbon–hydrogen frameworks.

questions.q: Which molecule is used directly by cells to drive energy-requiring processes such as muscle contraction and active transport?
questions.x: ATP releases energy when its terminal phosphate is removed, and this energy powers cell work directly. Glycogen and starch are stores that must first be broken down and respired to make ATP.

questions.q: A fatty acid has 18 carbon atoms in total and two C=C double bonds in its chain. Its formula is:
questions.x: The saturated C18 acid is C17H35COOH. Each C=C double bond removes two hydrogen atoms, so two double bonds give C17H31COOH (linoleic acid).

questions.q: One strand of a DNA molecule has a G + C content of 40%. The G + C content of its complementary strand is:
questions.x: Every G on one strand is opposite a C on the other, and every C opposite a G, so the G + C total is the same on both strands: 40%.

questions.q: Proteins show far greater variety of structure than polysaccharides such as starch mainly because proteins:
o: Are always larger than any polysaccharide
Are built from about 20 different monomers that can be joined in any order
Are joined by stronger bonds than glycosidic bonds
questions.x: With about 20 different amino acids arranged in any sequence, an almost unlimited number of proteins is possible. Starch is made of only one monomer, glucose, so its variety is limited.

questions.q: Water is often called a 'universal solvent' because it:
o: Dissolves every known substance, including fats
Reacts chemically with every substance placed in it
Dissolves more kinds of substances than any other common liquid
Is the only liquid found in living cells
questions.x: Water's polarity lets it dissolve a very wide range of ionic and polar substances. It does not dissolve non-polar substances such as fats and oils, so 'universal' is not literally true.

questions.q: In a beta pleated sheet, hydrogen bonds form between:
o: The R groups of distant amino acids only
Water molecules and the sugar units
The bases of two nucleotide strands
Neighbouring stretches of polypeptide chain lying side by side
questions.x: In a beta sheet, parts of the chain lie alongside each other, and C=O and N–H groups of neighbouring strands are hydrogen-bonded. In an alpha helix the bonds form within one coiled stretch.

questions.q: Which class of compounds typically contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with hydrogen and oxygen atoms in the ratio 2 : 1?
questions.x: Carbohydrates such as glucose (C6H12O6) have hydrogen and oxygen in the same 2 : 1 ratio as water. Lipids have much less oxygen, and proteins and nucleic acids also contain nitrogen.

questions.q: A DNA template strand reads 3′-TACGGATTC-5′. The mRNA transcribed from it reads:
questions.x: Each template base is paired with its RNA complement (T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C), giving 5′-AUGCCUAAG-3′. RNA has uracil, not thymine.

questions.q: The walls of cork cells become impermeable to water and gases because of the deposition of:
questions.x: Suberin, a waxy substance laid in the walls of cork cells, makes them waterproof. Pectin, cellulose and hemicellulose are normal wall components that let water pass.

questions.q: Compared with a typical plant cell, a typical animal cell has vacuoles that are:
o: Bounded by a tonoplast filled with cell sap
questions.x: Animal cells have small, often temporary vacuoles, such as food and water vacuoles. A single large central vacuole with cell sap is typical of mature plant cells.

questions.q: Microfilaments of the cytoskeleton, which help in cell movement and change of shape, are made of the protein:
questions.x: Microfilaments are thin actin fibres. Microtubules, by contrast, are made of tubulin.

questions.q: Plant cells usually have a fixed, regular shape, while animal cells are often irregular or rounded. This difference is mainly due to the:
o: Presence of centrioles in plant cells
Absence of a plasma membrane in animal cells
Rigid cell wall of plant cells
questions.x: The rigid cellulose wall holds a plant cell in a fixed shape. Animal cells have only a flexible plasma membrane, so their shape can vary.

questions.q: Most eukaryotic cells have a diameter in the range of about:
questions.x: Eukaryotic cells are typically 10–100 µm across, roughly ten times larger than most prokaryotic cells (about 1–10 µm).

questions.q: Receptors for touch, pressure, pain and temperature are present in large numbers in the:
questions.x: The skin contains Meissner's and Pacinian corpuscles, free nerve endings for pain and thermoreceptors. The retina, cochlea and olfactory epithelium hold receptors for light, sound and smell.

questions.q: A motor neuron, which has one axon and many dendrites arising from its cell body, is described as:
questions.x: Many processes leaving the cell body make a neuron multipolar. A bipolar neuron has just one dendrite and one axon.

questions.q: Which structure is part of the forebrain but NOT part of the cerebrum?
questions.x: The forebrain includes the cerebrum and the diencephalon. The hypothalamus belongs to the diencephalon, while the frontal lobe, cortex and corpus callosum are all parts of the cerebrum.

questions.q: Sensory neurons of spinal nerves have a single process leaving the cell body, which then splits into two branches. Such neurons are described as:
questions.x: One process leaving the cell body defines a unipolar neuron; it divides into a peripheral branch from the receptor and a central branch into the spinal cord.

questions.q: Unlike an electric current in a long wire, a nerve impulse does not get weaker as it travels along an axon because:
o: The myelin sheath adds energy to it
Neurotransmitter boosts it at every node
It is regenerated at each successive part of the membrane
The axon is a perfect electrical conductor
questions.x: Each region of membrane produces its own full-size action potential, so the impulse is renewed as it goes. The axoplasm is actually a poor conductor.

questions.q: In the developing embryo, the part that becomes the hindbrain is called the:
questions.x: The three embryonic divisions are the prosencephalon (forebrain), mesencephalon (midbrain) and rhombencephalon (hindbrain). The diencephalon is a part of the forebrain.

questions.q: Bright light makes the pupil narrow. Which cells detect the light and start this reflex?
questions.x: Light is detected by the rods and cones of the retina, which start the impulse. The circular muscles of the iris are the effector; the cornea and lens only focus light.

questions.q: On the back (dorsal side) of the midbrain are four rounded swellings called the:
questions.x: The corpora quadrigemina are four small swellings on the roof of the midbrain, linked with visual and auditory reflexes. Olfactory bulbs belong to the forebrain.

questions.q: In a pathway A → B → C, product C inhibits the first enzyme by feedback. A mutation makes this enzyme's allosteric site unable to bind C. The result is that:
o: C is overproduced, because the pathway is no longer switched off
No C can be made at all
The first enzyme can no longer bind A
questions.x: The active site is unaffected, so the pathway still runs, but C can no longer switch off the first enzyme, so C keeps being made even when plentiful.

questions.q: An irreversible inhibitor forms a covalent bond with an amino acid in an enzyme's active site. Adding a large amount of substrate will:
questions.x: Covalently bound inhibitors cannot be displaced by substrate, so the affected enzyme molecules stay inactive.

questions.q: A competitive inhibitor binds more strongly to the active site than the substrate does. To overcome its effect:
o: A lower substrate concentration is needed
A much higher substrate concentration is needed
Nothing can overcome it, even in theory
The temperature must be raised far above the optimum
questions.x: Competitive inhibition can be overcome by excess substrate, but the stronger the inhibitor binds, the more substrate is needed to win the competition.

questions.q: A single catalase molecule can break down millions of hydrogen peroxide molecules every second. This shows that enzymes are:
questions.x: Enzymes work extremely fast and are not consumed, so one molecule can convert huge numbers of substrate molecules. They lower, not raise, activation energy.

questions.q: According to Lamarck, wading birds such as herons have long legs because:
o: Their ancestors stretched their legs to keep their bodies dry in water
Herons with long legs caught more fish and left more offspring
Long legs were caused by a single mutation
The legs grew because of disuse
questions.x: Lamarck said the birds kept stretching their legs to avoid wetting their bodies, and the extra length was handed on. Selecting birds that already had longer legs is Darwinian.

questions.q: Before the first cells existed, molecules had to form without help from living things. Which of these was therefore NOT available to drive chemical evolution?
o: A source of energy such as lightning or ultraviolet light
Enzymes supplied by existing living cells
Simple gases such as methane and ammonia
Water in which molecules could collect
questions.x: Chemical evolution happened before life, so no enzymes from living cells were available. It needed raw gases, energy and water.

questions.q: Sidney Fox heated dry mixtures of amino acids and obtained protein-like chains. These were called:
questions.x: Fox called the heat-formed amino acid polymers proteinoids. When placed in water they formed small spheres called microspheres. Coacervates were Oparin's droplets.

questions.q: A student says, 'The bacteria became resistant because they needed to survive the antibiotic, and they passed this resistance on.' This explanation follows the idea of:
questions.x: Saying that a need produces a change which is then inherited is Lamarckian. In fact a few bacteria were already resistant and were selected, which is Darwin's natural selection.

questions.q: A blood test on day 3 of a woman's cycle shows low progesterone, low oestrogen and slowly rising FSH. Which stage does this match?
questions.x: Early in the cycle, the corpus luteum has gone, so both ovarian hormones are low and FSH rises to start new follicles growing. Before ovulation oestrogen would be high; in the luteal phase or pregnancy progesterone would be high.

questions.q: The level of oestrogen in the blood reaches its highest peak:
o: At the end of the luteal phase
Immediately after the corpus luteum degenerates
questions.x: The large Graafian follicle secretes a peak of oestrogen in the days just before ovulation. This peak triggers the LH surge.

questions.q: In the human female, the urethra:
o: Joins the vagina and carries urine and ova
Opens separately from the vagina and carries only urine
Carries both urine and menstrual fluid
questions.x: In the female, the urinary and reproductive openings are separate. In the male, the urethra carries both urine and semen.

questions.q: Which bone of the lower leg carries most of the body's weight?
questions.x: The tibia (shin bone) is the thick, weight-bearing bone of the lower leg. The slender fibula mainly gives attachment to muscles, and the radius is in the forearm.

questions.q: Adrenaline released during fright speeds up the heart and also widens the pupils. Which muscle types does it act on here?
questions.x: The heart wall is cardiac muscle, and the pupil is widened by smooth muscle of the iris. Neither effect involves skeletal muscle.

questions.q: Of the 206 bones of the adult human skeleton, the axial skeleton contains:
questions.x: The axial skeleton (skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum, hyoid) has 80 bones. The remaining 126 make up the appendicular skeleton of the limbs and girdles.

questions.q: Artery walls contain smooth muscle rather than skeletal muscle. An advantage of this is that the muscle:
o: Contracts faster than any other muscle
Can stay contracted for long periods without tiring or conscious effort
questions.x: Vessel diameter must be adjusted all day without our thinking about it. Smooth muscle is involuntary and keeps up slow, sustained contraction without fatigue. All muscle needs ATP.

questions.q: Which feature is found in smooth muscle but NOT in skeletal muscle?
questions.x: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped, tapering at both ends. Striations, many nuclei and somatic nerve control are features of skeletal muscle.

questions.q: In the hip joint, the head of the femur fits into the:
questions.x: The acetabulum is the deep cup-shaped socket of the hip bone that holds the head of the femur. The glenoid cavity is the shoulder's socket, and the obturator foramen is an opening, not a socket.

questions.q: The stomach wall stretches greatly after a meal and then contracts slowly to churn the food. Its muscle layers are:
questions.x: The wall of the stomach contains layers of smooth muscle, which can be stretched a lot and contract slowly and involuntarily to mix food.

questions.q: Osteoclasts break down bone matrix by secreting:
o: Acid and enzymes that dissolve mineral and collagen
questions.x: Osteoclasts release acid, which dissolves the mineral, and enzymes, which digest collagen. Secreting collagen and calcium salts is the work of osteoblasts.

questions.q: Which statement about gene linkage is NOT correct?
o: Linked genes always assort independently of each other
Linked genes lie on the same chromosome
Linked genes tend to be inherited together
Linkage can be broken by crossing over
questions.x: Linked genes lie on one chromosome and tend to stay together, which is why they do not assort independently. Crossing over can separate them.

questions.q: A test cross uses a dihybrid in repulsion, Ab/aB, whose genes recombine with a frequency of 20%. Offspring showing both dominant traits should make up:
questions.x: In repulsion, AB is a recombinant gamete. Recombinants total 20%, split equally between AB and ab, so AB gametes and hence AaBb offspring are 10%.

questions.q: Chiasmata hold the homologous chromosomes of a bivalent together until they separate at:
questions.x: Homologues stay joined at chiasmata through metaphase I and separate at anaphase I. Anaphase II separates sister chromatids, not homologues.

questions.q: A heterozygous red-eyed female Drosophila is crossed with a red-eyed male. The offspring are expected to be:
o: All daughters red-eyed; half the sons white-eyed
Half the daughters and half the sons white-eyed
All sons white-eyed; all daughters red-eyed
questions.x: Every daughter gets the father's red X, so all are red-eyed. Sons get one of the mother's two X chromosomes, so half are white-eyed.

questions.q: A hemophilic man and a carrier woman have a son with hemophilia. From whom did the son inherit the hemophilia allele?
o: Both his father and his mother
Neither; it is a new mutation in the son
questions.x: A son receives his X only from his mother; the father gives him a Y. So even with a hemophilic father, the son's allele came from his carrier mother.

questions.q: Which of the following human disorders is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait?
questions.x: Duchenne muscular dystrophy, like hemophilia and colour blindness, is X-linked recessive. Albinism and phenylketonuria are autosomal recessive, and hairy ear rims are Y-linked.

questions.q: Round green and wrinkled yellow seeds appeared in Mendel's dihybrid F2, although the original parents were round yellow and wrinkled green. This shows that:
o: Round and yellow are always inherited together
Mutations arose in the F1 plants
The genes for seed shape and seed colour are sorted into gametes independently
Seed colour depends on seed shape
questions.x: New combinations appear because the alleles for shape and for colour separate independently at gamete formation. If round always went with yellow, these new types could not arise.

questions.q: In which of these groups is the female the heterogametic sex?
questions.x: In birds the female is ZW and makes two kinds of eggs. In mammals and Drosophila the male is XY, and in grasshoppers the male is XO.

questions.q: The SA node is called the pacemaker of the heart because it:
o: Is the largest mass of muscle in the heart
Is the only part of the heart supplied by nerves
Delays the impulse between atria and ventricles
Produces impulses at the fastest rate and so sets the rhythm of the whole heart
questions.x: The SA node fires faster than any other heart tissue, so it starts every beat and sets the heart rate. Delaying the impulse is the job of the AV node.

questions.q: The atrioventricular valves close at the start of ventricular systole because:
o: Pressure in the ventricles rises above pressure in the atria
Pressure in the aorta rises above pressure in the ventricles
The papillary muscles pull the cusps shut
The atria contract and push the cusps closed
questions.x: As the ventricles contract, their pressure exceeds atrial pressure and pushes the cusps shut. Papillary muscles and chordae only stop the cusps turning inside out; they do not close them.

questions.q: In the capillaries of a working muscle, which substances pass from the blood into the tissue fluid?
o: Plasma proteins and red blood cells
questions.x: Oxygen and nutrients such as glucose diffuse out to the cells. Carbon dioxide and wastes pass the other way, and cells and large proteins stay in the blood.

questions.q: If someone's pulse is 60 per minute, how long does each heartbeat take?
questions.x: One cycle lasts 60 seconds ÷ 60 beats = 1.0 second. The figure 0.8 second applies to a rate of 75 beats per minute.

questions.q: Which is a secondary lymphoid organ, where mature lymphocytes meet antigens?
questions.x: Bone marrow and thymus are primary organs where lymphocytes form or mature. Lymph nodes (and the spleen) are secondary organs where mature lymphocytes meet antigens.

questions.q: Memory cells, which allow a faster response on a second infection, are formed by:
questions.x: Activated B cells give rise to memory B cells and activated T cells give rise to memory T cells, so both arms of the specific response have memory.

questions.q: The BCG vaccine is given to protect against:
questions.x: BCG (Bacillus Calmette–Guérin) is the vaccine against tuberculosis, usually given at birth.

questions.q: Only a very small part of the oxygen in blood is carried dissolved in the plasma because:
o: Oxygen is poorly soluble in water
Plasma is too acidic to hold oxygen
questions.x: Oxygen dissolves only slightly in water, so plasma alone could carry far too little. Haemoglobin in red cells raises the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood many times over.

questions.q: After deliberately breathing very fast and deep for a minute, a person may stop breathing for a short time without discomfort. This is because:
o: The carbon dioxide level of the blood has fallen, so the respiratory centre is less stimulated
The blood has become saturated with carbon dioxide
The diaphragm muscle is fatigued and cannot contract
The oxygen level of the blood has fallen sharply
questions.x: Over-breathing washes carbon dioxide out of the blood. As CO₂ is the main stimulus for breathing, the drive to breathe falls until CO₂ builds up again. Blood oxygen actually rises slightly, not falls.

questions.q: The instrument used to measure lung volumes such as tidal volume and vital capacity is the:
questions.x: A spirometer records the volume of air breathed in and out. A sphygmomanometer measures blood pressure and a haemocytometer is used to count blood cells.

questions.q: Excess amino acids cannot be stored. In the liver their amino groups are removed and turned into urea. Removal of the amino group is called:
questions.x: Deamination removes the amino group, which becomes ammonia and is then converted into urea; the rest of the molecule can be used for energy. Emulsification is the action of bile on fats.

questions.q: Trypsin from the pancreas breaks proteins into smaller peptides. It works in the:
o: Alkaline conditions of the small intestine
Acidic conditions of the large intestine
questions.x: Trypsin acts in the duodenum, where bicarbonate from pancreatic juice and bile makes the contents alkaline. This is the opposite of pepsin, which needs the acid of the stomach.

questions.q: The cystic duct connects the:
o: Gall bladder to the common bile duct
questions.x: The cystic duct leads from the gall bladder and joins the hepatic duct from the liver to form the common bile duct, which opens into the duodenum.

questions.q: The podocytes of Bowman's capsule help filtration because their foot-like processes:
o: Actively pump glucose into the capsule
Leave narrow filtration slits through which the filtrate passes
Form a waterproof seal around the glomerulus
Secrete hydrogen ions into the filtrate
questions.x: Podocytes wrap the glomerular capillaries with interlocking foot processes. The narrow slits between them let water and small solutes through while holding back larger particles.

questions.q: On a hot day, a plant can lower the temperature of its leaves mainly by:
o: Transpiration, as evaporation of water from the leaves removes heat
questions.x: Evaporation of water during transpiration takes latent heat from the leaf, cooling it. Closing stomata would stop this cooling.

questions.q: Heatstroke occurs when:
o: The hypothalamic set point falls below normal
Shivering raises the body temperature slightly
Skin arterioles constrict in cold air
The body's cooling fails and core temperature rises to a dangerous level
questions.x: In heatstroke, heat gain exceeds heat loss and sweating may fail, so core temperature climbs high enough to damage proteins and the brain.

questions.q: Compared with excreting ammonia, excreting urea:
o: Uses more water and needs no energy
Saves water but costs energy to make
Is more toxic to the body
Can only take place through gills
questions.x: Urea is less toxic and can be concentrated, saving water, but making it in the ornithine cycle uses ATP.

questions.q: Which of these properties correctly describes urea?
o: It is insoluble and passed as a paste
It is the most toxic nitrogenous waste
It is soluble in water and much less toxic than ammonia
It is made mainly in the kidneys
questions.x: Urea dissolves easily so it is carried in plasma and urine, and it is far less toxic than ammonia. It is made in the liver, not the kidneys.

questions.q: Urine leaves the body from the bladder through the:
questions.x: The urethra carries urine from the bladder to the outside. Each ureter carries urine from a kidney down to the bladder.

questions.q: The renal cortex looks granular because it contains:
o: The renal pyramids and long loops of Henle
Large numbers of renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules
questions.x: All the glomeruli with their capsules, and the coiled PCTs and DCTs, lie in the cortex and give it a dotted look. The straight loops and collecting ducts make the medulla look striped.

questions.q: A person sitting on a cold stone bench loses heat to it mainly by:
questions.x: Conduction is heat transfer by direct contact between the body and a colder solid surface.

questions.q: High blood pressure can be a result of kidney failure, not only a cause. It results because failing kidneys:
o: Retain salt and water, so blood volume increases
Remove too much water from the blood
Release all their nephrons into the blood
questions.x: When the kidneys cannot excrete enough salt and water, the extra fluid raises blood volume and therefore blood pressure.

questions.q: Fetal DNA is tested with two probes. The probe for the sickle-cell allele binds, but the probe for the normal haemoglobin allele does not. The fetus is:
questions.x: Since only the sickle-cell probe binds, the fetus has no normal allele and two sickle-cell alleles. A carrier would bind both probes; a normal homozygote would bind only the normal probe.

questions.q: In genetic engineering, 'gene cloning' means:
o: Producing a whole new animal from a body cell
Changing the base sequence of a gene at random
Cutting a gene into many small pieces
Making many identical copies of a gene by letting host cells that contain it multiply
questions.x: Each time a transformed bacterium divides, its recombinant plasmid is copied, so a colony holds millions of copies of the inserted gene. Producing a whole animal from a body cell is reproductive cloning, a different process.

questions.q: A linear DNA molecule contains three recognition sites for a particular restriction enzyme. Complete digestion with this enzyme will give how many fragments?
questions.x: Each cut in a linear molecule adds one more piece, so three cuts give four fragments. A circular plasmid with three sites would give only three fragments.

questions.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, 6 g of hydrogen reacts with excess nitrogen and 17 g of ammonia is collected. What is the percentage yield? (N = 14, H = 1)
questions.x: H₂ = 6/2 = 3 mol, and the ratio H₂ : NH₃ = 3 : 2 gives 2 mol NH₃ = 34 g in theory. Yield = 17/34 × 100 = 50%.

questions.q: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 50 g, and 40 g of product is collected. What is the percentage yield?
questions.x: Percentage yield = (actual ÷ theoretical) × 100 = (40/50) × 100 = 80%. 125% comes from inverting the fraction.

questions.q: Light of frequency 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz delivers a total of 6.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ J to a detector. With h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, the number of photons received is:
questions.x: Energy of one photon = hν = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5 × 10¹⁴ = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Number = 6.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ / 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 200.

questions.q: The energy of a photon in terms of its wave number ν̄ is:
questions.x: Wave number ν̄ = 1/λ, so E = hc/λ = hcν̄. Energy is directly proportional to wave number.

questions.q: How many atomic orbitals contain at least one electron in a ground-state sodium atom (Z = 11)?
questions.x: Na is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. Occupied orbitals: 1s, 2s, three 2p and 3s = 6. Four is the number of occupied subshells, not orbitals.

questions.q: A sealed 8.21 dm³ cylinder at 400 K holds a gas at a pressure of 2 atm. Taking R as 0.0821 in these units, how much gas does it contain, in moles?
Which gas has the smallest van der Waals constant a?
questions.x: a measures the attractive forces between molecules. Helium atoms are small, non-polar and hard to polarise, so their attractions are the weakest; NH₃, with hydrogen bonding, has a large a.

questions.q: For a fixed amount of gas kept at constant volume, the ideal gas equation shows that:
questions.x: From PV = nRT, P/T = nR/V. With n and V fixed, P/T is constant, so pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

questions.q: A sample of gas has a volume of 12 dm³ at 1 atm. At the same temperature, which pair of pressure and volume could also belong to this sample?
questions.x: At constant temperature PV stays at 1 × 12 = 12 dm³ atm. Only 3 atm × 4 dm³ gives 12; the others give 108, 20 and 16.

questions.q: At 100 °C, the vapour pressure of pure water is:
questions.x: Water boils at 100 °C at 1 atm, and at the boiling point vapour pressure equals the external pressure, 760 mm Hg.

questions.q: A unit cell has a = b ≠ c and α = β = γ = 90°. It belongs to the:
questions.x: Two equal edges, one different, and all angles 90° define the tetragonal system. Cubic needs all three edges equal.

questions.q: For KCl (kJ mol⁻¹): ΔHf = −437; sublimation of K = +89; ½ dissociation of Cl₂ = +122; ionisation energy of K = +419; electron affinity of Cl = −349. The lattice energy for K⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → KCl(s) is:
questions.x: Sum of other steps = 89 + 122 + 419 − 349 = +281; lattice energy = −437 − 281 = −718 kJ mol⁻¹. Taking the electron affinity as +349 gives the wrong −1416.

questions.q: For CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) in a closed vessel, increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium:
o: To the right, as more solid forms
To the left, as the only gas is on the right
Not at all, as solids are present
To the right, as Kc increases
questions.x: Only CO₂ is a gas, and it is on the right. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles, so CaCO₃ re-forms.

questions.q: When a reversible reaction is started with reactants only, the rate of the reverse reaction at the very start is:
questions.x: No products are present at the start, so the reverse reaction cannot occur yet. Its rate rises as products build up.

questions.q: Which of these claims about a system at equilibrium is NOT true?
o: At equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions stop
It can be reached from either the reactant side or the product side
It is set up only in a closed system
The concentrations stay constant at constant temperature
questions.x: Equilibrium is dynamic: both reactions go on at equal rates. The other three statements are true.

questions.q: The rate of reaction in terms of a reactant R is written as −Δ[R]/Δt. The minus sign is included because:
o: [R] decreases with time, and the rate must be a positive quantity
The reverse reaction is faster than the forward reaction
questions.x: Δ[R] is negative for a reactant since it is used up; the minus sign makes the rate positive. It has nothing to do with ΔH or k.

questions.q: A student measures how the concentration of H₂O₂ falls every minute as it decomposes. This study belongs to the branch of chemistry called:
questions.x: Chemical kinetics studies how fast reactions go and how rates change with time. Thermochemistry deals with heat changes, not speeds.

questions.q: The enthalpy of a reaction is the heat change when:
o: 1 g of each reactant reacts at constant volume
The moles of reactants shown in the balanced equation react completely at constant pressure
The reaction reaches equilibrium at constant volume
One mole of product is formed from its elements
questions.x: ΔH of reaction refers to the amounts in the balanced equation, at constant pressure. Forming one mole from elements is the special case of enthalpy of formation.

questions.q: For 2X → Y, ΔH = −40 kJ. What is ΔH for 4X → 2Y?
questions.x: Multiplying an equation by 2 doubles its ΔH: 2 × (−40) = −80 kJ. The sign changes only when the equation is reversed.

questions.q: When dilute NaOH is added to dilute HCl, the temperature of the mixture rises from 25 °C to 31 °C. The reaction is:
questions.x: Heat released by the reaction warms the solution, so the reaction is exothermic and ΔH is negative.

questions.q: Copper reacts with hot concentrated sulphuric acid: Cu + 2H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + SO₂ + 2H₂O. What fraction of the H₂SO₄ molecules acts as the oxidising agent?
questions.x: Only the sulphur that becomes SO₂ is reduced (+6 to +4); the other H₂SO₄ forms CuSO₄ with S still +6. So 1 of every 2 molecules is the oxidising agent.

questions.q: In Br₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O → 2HBr + H₂SO₄, the reducing agent is:
questions.x: Sulphur rises from +4 in SO₂ to +6 in H₂SO₄, so SO₂ is oxidised and is the reducing agent; bromine is reduced from 0 to −1.

questions.q: Non-polar covalent substances such as methane and tetrachloromethane have low melting and boiling points because:
o: Their covalent bonds are very weak
They contain ions held by strong forces
Only weak forces act between their molecules
questions.x: Melting and boiling separate molecules, not break covalent bonds. Between non-polar molecules there are only weak intermolecular forces, so little energy is needed.

questions.q: CCl₄ is non-polar but CHCl₃ is polar. The reason is that in CHCl₃:
o: The molecule is planar instead of tetrahedral
The carbon atom has a lone pair
Replacing one Cl by H makes the bond dipoles unequal, so they no longer cancel
questions.x: Both are tetrahedral. In CCl₄ four identical C–Cl dipoles cancel; in CHCl₃ the C–H dipole is different from the C–Cl dipoles, leaving a net dipole moment.

questions.q: A molecule XY₃ is found to be trigonal planar. What can be concluded about the central atom X?
o: It has three bond pairs and no lone pair
It has three bond pairs and one lone pair
It has two bond pairs and one lone pair
It has four bond pairs and no lone pair
questions.x: Three bond pairs alone spread out at 120° in a plane. A lone pair as well would push the bonds down into a pyramid, as in NH₃.

questions.q: The bond energies of the hydrogen halides fall in the order H–F > H–Cl > H–Br > H–I. This is because, from HF to HI:
o: The bond length decreases as the halogen atom gets smaller
The number of bonds between the atoms decreases
The bond length increases as the halogen atom gets larger
questions.x: Larger halogen atoms give longer bonds with poorer orbital overlap, so the bond becomes weaker; HI is the easiest to break.

questions.q: Which pair of gaseous ions has the same number of unpaired electrons?
questions.x: Ti³⁺ is 3d¹ and Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹, and each has one unpaired electron. V³⁺ has 2, Cr³⁺ has 3, Mn²⁺ has 5 and Ni²⁺ has 2.

questions.q: Solutions of most organic compounds, such as glucose or urea in water, do not conduct electricity because:
o: They contain too many oxygen atoms
They react with water to form metals
Their molecules are too heavy to move
The compounds are covalent and do not ionise in solution
questions.x: Conduction in solution needs free ions. Most organic compounds are covalent non-electrolytes and stay as neutral molecules.

questions.q: Coal tar, obtained by the destructive distillation of coal, is an important source of:
o: Aromatic compounds such as benzene, phenol and naphthalene
Natural gas consisting mainly of methane
questions.x: Heating coal strongly in the absence of air gives coal gas, coal tar and coke. Coal tar is rich in aromatic compounds.

questions.q: The molecular formula of benzene hexachloride (BHC) is:
questions.x: Three molecules of Cl₂ add across the benzene ring without removing any hydrogen: C₆H₆ + 3Cl₂ → C₆H₆Cl₆.

questions.q: Which condensed formula represents hex-3-yne?
questions.x: Hex-3-yne has six carbons with the triple bond between C3 and C4, which is in the middle of the chain. The last formula is an alkene.

questions.q: Which sequence converts methylbenzene mainly into 4-nitrobenzoic acid?
o: Oxidise with hot KMnO₄ first, then nitrate
Nitrate first, then oxidise the side chain with hot KMnO₄
questions.x: –CH₃ is ortho/para-directing, so nitration gives 4-nitromethylbenzene (plus the 2-isomer); oxidation then turns –CH₃ into –COOH. Oxidising first gives –COOH, a meta-director, leading to 3-nitrobenzoic acid.

questions.q: How many σ bonds are present in one molecule of benzene, C₆H₆?
questions.x: Benzene has six C–C σ bonds in the ring and six C–H σ bonds, a total of 12. The π electrons are delocalised over the ring.

questions.q: An alkyne has two isopropyl groups joined to the carbons of a triple bond, (CH₃)₂CH–C≡C–CH(CH₃)₂. Its IUPAC name is:
questions.x: The longest chain through the triple bond has six carbons, with the triple bond at C3. The methyl branches are on C2 and C5 from either end.

questions.q: Ethene reacts with bromine by electrophilic addition, and benzene reacts with bromine (with FeBr₃) by electrophilic substitution. In both reactions:
o: A nucleophile attacks a carbon atom
An electrophile attacks the π electrons of the hydrocarbon
Free radicals are formed by light
A hydrogen atom is first removed by a base
questions.x: The π electrons of ethene and of benzene act as an electron source, so both are attacked by electrophiles. They differ only in what happens to the intermediate.

questions.q: Benzene is treated with chlorine in the presence of anhydrous FeCl₃ in the dark. The products are:
questions.x: With a Lewis acid catalyst and no light, chlorine substitutes one ring H: C₆H₆ + Cl₂ → C₆H₅Cl + HCl. Addition to give BHC needs sunlight and no catalyst.

questions.q: The compound CH₂Cl₂, commonly called methylene chloride, is named in the IUPAC system as:
questions.x: It is methane with two hydrogens replaced by chlorine, so it is dichloromethane. Methene does not exist as a parent name, and the compound has only one carbon, so it is not an ethane.

questions.q: X dissolves in aqueous NaOH but gives no gas with NaHCO₃ solution. Y does not dissolve in aqueous NaOH but gives hydrogen with sodium. X and Y could be:
questions.x: Phenol is acidic enough to react with NaOH but too weak to release CO₂ from NaHCO₃, which fits X; ethanoic acid would give CO₂. Ethanol reacts with sodium but not with aqueous NaOH, which fits Y.

questions.q: Phenol is only moderately soluble in cold water. Which statement best explains this?
o: Its –OH group hydrogen-bonds with water, but the large C₆H₅ group is non-polar
It reacts with water to form phenoxide ions completely
It has no polar bonds, so it cannot interact with water
It forms ionic bonds with water molecules
questions.x: The –OH group can hydrogen-bond to water, giving some solubility, while the bulky hydrophobic benzene ring limits it. Phenol is only a weak acid, so very little ionises.

questions.q: The IUPAC name of the ether CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₂CH₃ is:
questions.x: Ethers are named as alkoxyalkanes, with the larger alkyl group as the parent chain: propane carrying an ethoxy group on C-1. 'Propoxyethane' wrongly makes the smaller group the parent.

questions.q: Methyl propyl ketone, CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃, is named by IUPAC rules as:
questions.x: The chain has five carbons and the C=O is given the lowest number, C-2, so it is pentan-2-one. 'Pentan-4-one' numbers from the wrong end.

questions.q: Aldehydes and ketones boil higher than alkanes, but lower than alcohols, of similar molar mass. This is because their molecules:
o: Hydrogen-bond to each other more strongly than alcohols do
Have dipole–dipole attractions but cannot hydrogen-bond to each other
Are ionic in the liquid state
questions.x: The polar C=O group gives dipole–dipole forces, stronger than the dispersion forces of alkanes. They have no H on oxygen, so they cannot hydrogen-bond among themselves as alcohols do.

questions.q: Ethanoic acid ionises in water: CH₃COOH + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺. The conjugate base of ethanoic acid is:
questions.x: Removing H⁺ from CH₃COOH gives CH₃COO⁻, its conjugate base. H₃O⁺ is the conjugate acid of water.

questions.q: Among the main classes of food, proteins are the major dietary source of the element:
questions.x: Carbohydrates and fats contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, while every amino acid contains nitrogen in its amino group.

questions.q: Basic (cationic) dyes, whose coloured part carries a positive charge, are mainly used to dye:
questions.x: Acrylic fibres carry negative groups that attract the positive dye ions. On cotton, basic dyes need a mordant such as tannin, and polyester takes disperse dyes.

questions.q: Vector P = 3î − 2ĵ + k̂ and vector Q = 2î + 4ĵ + 2k̂. The angle between P and Q is:
questions.x: P · Q = (3)(2) + (−2)(4) + (1)(2) = 6 − 8 + 2 = 0. A zero scalar product of non-zero vectors means they are perpendicular.

questions.q: A 0.1 kg ball falling at 20 m s⁻¹ hits the ground and comes to rest without bouncing. The impulse given to the ball by the ground is:
questions.x: Impulse = change in momentum = 0 − (0.1 × 20 downward) = 2 N s upward. The ground pushes up, opposite to the ball's original motion.

questions.q: A car covers 150 m along a straight road in 10 s without changing direction. The magnitude of its average velocity is:
questions.x: Average velocity = displacement ÷ time = 150 m ÷ 10 s = 15 m s⁻¹. With no change of direction, displacement equals distance.

questions.q: A rope pulls a 10 kg box across a floor with a horizontal force of 50 N. The friction force on the box is 20 N. The acceleration of the box is:
questions.x: Net force = 50 − 20 = 30 N, so a = 30 ÷ 10 = 3 m s⁻². 5 m s⁻² ignores friction.

questions.q: The total time a projectile spends in flight over level ground, for launch speed v at angle θ above the horizontal, is (no air drag):
questions.x: Vertical displacement returns to zero when (v sin θ)t − ½gt² = 0, giving t = 2v sin θ / g. v sin θ / g is only the time to the top, and v² sin 2θ / g is the range.

questions.q: Cars are built with crumple zones that fold up in a crash. They reduce the force on passengers because they:
o: Reduce the car's change in momentum to zero
Increase the car's mass during the crash
Increase the time over which the car's momentum changes
Reduce the time of the collision
questions.x: For a given change in momentum, F = Δp/Δt, so a longer stopping time means a smaller average force. The change in momentum itself is not reduced.

questions.q: Two trolleys of 1 kg and 3 kg are held together with a compressed spring between them and then released. At one instant the 1 kg trolley has an acceleration of 6 m s⁻². At that instant the 3 kg trolley has an acceleration of:
o: 6 m s⁻² in the opposite direction
18 m s⁻² in the opposite direction
2 m s⁻² in the same direction
2 m s⁻² in the opposite direction
questions.x: The spring pushes on both with equal and opposite forces: F = 1 × 6 = 6 N. For the 3 kg trolley a = 6 ÷ 3 = 2 m s⁻², in the opposite direction.

questions.q: An engine wastes 300 J out of every 1000 J of energy it takes in. Its efficiency is:
questions.x: Useful output = 1000 − 300 = 700 J. Efficiency = 700 ÷ 1000 × 100% = 70%. 30% is the fraction wasted.

questions.q: One electron-volt (eV), a unit used for very small energies, is equal to:
questions.x: 1 eV is the energy gained by an electron moving through a potential difference of 1 V: (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(1 V) = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. 3.6 × 10⁶ J is one kilowatt-hour.

questions.q: When a body is lifted at constant speed, the work done against gravity is stored in the body as:
questions.x: At constant speed the kinetic energy does not change, so the work done against gravity is stored as gravitational potential energy.

questions.q: Angular velocity of a rotating body is defined as the:
o: Rate of change of linear velocity
Product of radius and angular displacement
Rate of change of angular displacement
questions.x: Angular velocity ω = Δθ/Δt, the rate at which angular displacement changes. Rate of change of linear velocity is linear acceleration.

questions.q: At the instant a raindrop is released from rest in still air, the air drag on it is:
o: Zero, because its speed is zero
questions.x: Drag depends on speed (F = 6πηrv for a small drop), so at v = 0 the drag is zero and the drop starts with acceleration g. Drag grows only as the drop speeds up.

questions.q: The viscosity of a fluid is a measure of its:
o: Internal friction, which resists the sliding of one layer over another
Density, or mass per unit volume
Ability to be compressed under pressure
Surface tension at its free surface
questions.x: Viscosity is the internal friction between adjacent layers of a fluid; it is what causes fluid drag. Density and compressibility are different properties.

questions.q: An oil line (bore 5 × 10⁻⁴ m²) carries oil, ρ = 800 kg m⁻³, moving at 2 m s⁻¹. How many kilograms of oil are delivered in 10 seconds?
questions.x: Mass flow rate = ρAv = 800 × 5 × 10⁻⁴ × 2 = 0.8 kg s⁻¹, so in 10 s the mass is 8 kg. Forgetting the time gives 0.8 kg.

questions.q: The particular speed above which the smooth motion of a viscous fluid breaks up into eddies is called the:
questions.x: Below the critical velocity the flow is laminar; above it the flow becomes turbulent. Terminal velocity is the steady speed of a falling body.

questions.q: Newton's formula gives the speed of sound in a gas of density 2.5 kg m⁻³ as 200 m s⁻¹. The pressure of the gas is:
questions.x: From v = √(P/ρ), P = v²ρ = (200)² × 2.5 = 4 × 10⁴ × 2.5 = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Not squaring v gives 500 Pa.

questions.q: In a stationary wave, the energy of the vibrating medium is:
o: Carried steadily along the medium at the wave speed
Stored within each loop, changing between kinetic and potential forms
questions.x: Because the two component waves carry equal energy in opposite directions, nothing flows along the medium. Within each loop energy changes between kinetic (string passing straight) and potential (string at its extreme shape).

questions.q: On a hot day the temperature of the air inside an organ pipe rises. The frequency of the note produced by the pipe:
o: Stays the same, because the length is fixed
Increases, because the speed of sound increases
questions.x: The wavelength is fixed by the pipe length, but the speed of sound rises with temperature, so f = v/λ increases.

questions.q: A mass oscillating on a spring has a time period T. If the mass is made 4 times as large with the same spring, the period becomes:
questions.x: T = 2π√(m/k), so T ∝ √m. Four times the mass gives √4 = 2 times the period.

questions.q: Transverse waves move at 160 m s⁻¹ on a sitar wire whose vibrating length is 0.4 m. If the wire vibrates in two loops, its frequency is:
questions.x: Two loops make one whole wavelength, so λ = 0.4 m and f = v/λ = 160/0.4 = 400 Hz. This is the second harmonic; the fundamental is 200 Hz.

questions.q: Sound travels at 340 m s⁻¹ in still air. A steady wind blows at 10 m s⁻¹ from a source towards a listener. The speed of the sound relative to the ground, on its way to the listener, is:
questions.x: Sound moves at 340 m s⁻¹ through the air, and the wind carries the air towards the listener, so relative to the ground the speeds add: 340 + 10 = 350 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: According to the first law of thermodynamics, the total energy of an isolated system:
questions.x: An isolated system exchanges no heat or work with its surroundings, so by conservation of energy its total energy stays the same.

questions.q: A gas is taken round a complete cycle that forms a closed loop on a pressure–volume graph. The net work done by the gas in one cycle equals the:
o: Area under the upper part of the loop only
Highest pressure multiplied by the lowest volume
questions.x: The work done in expansion minus the work done on the gas in compression equals the area inside the loop on the P–V graph.

questions.q: How much charge per square metre must sit on a big metal plate to give a field of 2 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹ next to it? (Use E = σ/ε₀, ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² SI units)
questions.x: σ = ε₀E = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 2 × 10⁵ = 1.77 × 10⁻⁶ C m⁻². Using σ/2ε₀ would give the smaller value 8.85 × 10⁻⁷.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a unit of energy?
questions.x: The volt is energy per unit charge (J C⁻¹), a unit of potential. The joule, electronvolt and kilowatt-hour all measure energy.

questions.q: For a capacitor discharging through a resistor, a graph of the charge on the capacitor against time is:
o: A straight line falling to zero
A curve rising steeply at first, then levelling off
A curve falling steeply at first, then more and more slowly towards zero
questions.x: Discharge is exponential: the charge falls fastest at the start, when the current is largest, and approaches zero more and more slowly.

questions.q: A charged capacitor discharges through a resistor. The current in the resistor:
o: Is zero at the start and increases steadily
Stays constant until the capacitor is empty
Is largest at the start and decreases gradually to zero
questions.x: As the capacitor loses charge its voltage falls, so the current V/R falls too. The decay is exponential, from a maximum at the start towards zero.

questions.q: In 2 seconds, 5 × 10¹⁸ electrons flow through a cross-section of a conductor. What current does this represent? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.x: Q = ne = 5 × 10¹⁸ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 0.8 C. I = Q/t = 0.8 ÷ 2 = 0.4 A. 0.8 A forgets to divide by the time.

questions.q: Magnetic flux density and vector area are both vectors, yet magnetic flux is a scalar. This is because flux is their:
questions.x: The dot (scalar) product of two vectors gives a scalar: Φ = B · A. A cross product would give another vector.

questions.q: A charged particle moves in a circle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. The centripetal force it needs is supplied by the:
o: Magnetic force on the moving charge
Electric force from the magnet's poles
questions.x: The magnetic force qvB is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it acts as the centripetal force: qvB = mv²/r.

questions.q: In 0.1 s, the flux linking each of 500 turns changes by 2 × 10⁻³ Wb. What average emf appears across the coil?
questions.x: ε = N ΔΦ/Δt = 500 × 2 × 10⁻³/0.1 = 10 V. Leaving out the number of turns gives 0.02 V.

questions.q: Two alternating quantities of the same frequency are said to be in phase when they:
o: Are produced by the same generator
Reach their maximum and zero values at the same instants
questions.x: Being in phase means a zero phase difference: both pass through zero and reach their peaks together. Equal peak values are not required.

questions.q: A diode made from germanium begins to conduct appreciably once the forward voltage across it exceeds roughly:
questions.x: The barrier potential of a germanium junction is about 0.3 V; 0.7 V is the value for silicon.

questions.q: In the particle model of light, the momentum of a photon of wavelength λ is:
questions.x: A photon's momentum is p = E/c = hf/c = h/λ, even though its rest mass is zero.

questions.q: The ground state of an atom is:
o: The state in which it has been ionised
Any state with energy above zero
The highest energy level an electron can reach
questions.x: The ground state (n = 1 for hydrogen) is the lowest energy level. Higher levels are excited states, and removing the electron is ionisation.

questions.q: A magnesium ion, ²⁴₁₂Mg²⁺, contains:
questions.x: Z = 12 protons and N = 24 − 12 = 12 neutrons. The 2+ charge means two electrons have been lost, leaving 10. Gaining electrons would give a negative ion.

questions.q: Ali's aunt kept her best china plates in a glass cabinet and never used them, not even at Eid. When Ali asked why, she smiled and said the plates had come with her from her mother's house fifty years ago, and that every chip would feel like losing a piece of her mother. Why does Ali's aunt not use the plates?
o: They remind her of her mother and she fears damaging them
They are too small for serving a large family
She bought them recently and is saving them
questions.x: She links the plates to her mother and says a chip would feel like a loss, so she protects them. They are fifty years old, not new, and no chips are mentioned.

questions.q: When the results were announced, the hockey team was jubilant. The players lifted their coach onto their shoulders, danced around the ground and sang all the way back to the hostel. Even the quietest boy on the team was shouting and laughing. As used in the passage, 'jubilant' means:
questions.x: Dancing, singing and shouting with laughter show great happiness, so 'jubilant' means full of joy. 'Quietly proud' does not fit such noisy celebration.

questions.q: Which sentence places 'hardly' correctly?
questions.x: 'Hardly' is a negative adverb of degree that goes after the auxiliary and before the main verb; if placed first it would need inversion.

questions.q: Choose the correct form: "The new flyover is said ___ last year."
questions.x: The completion happened before now and the flyover is the receiver of the action, so the perfect passive infinitive is needed.

questions.q: In which sentence is 'hard' used as an adverb?
o: The ground was hard after the frost.
Hamza works hard for his exams.
It was a hard decision to make.
questions.x: In the first sentence 'hard' tells how he works, so it modifies the verb; in the others it describes a noun as an adjective.

questions.q: Choose the correct verb: "Sara wishes she ___ the chance to study abroad last year."
questions.x: A wish about the past takes the past perfect; here the verb is 'have', so the past perfect is 'had had'.

questions.q: Choose the correct preposition: "Nobody spoke ___ the lecture; everyone was taking notes."
questions.x: 'During' shows that something happens within a period or event.

questions.q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "She is good both at chemistry as well as physics."
o: She is good both at chemistry and as well as physics.
She is good at both chemistry and physics.
She is good at both chemistry as well as physics.
She is both good at chemistry as well as at physics.
questions.x: 'Both' is paired with 'and', never with 'as well as', and it should come just before the two things joined: 'at both chemistry and physics'.

questions.q: Choose the correct word: "The new medicine had no ____ on his fever."
questions.x: After 'no', a noun is needed: 'effect' means a result. 'Affect' is normally a verb, and 'effective' and 'effectively' are adjective and adverb forms.

questions.q: Sara says students need more sleep before exams. Hamza replies, "So Sara wants us to sleep all day and never study!" What is wrong with Hamza's reply?
o: He agrees with Sara but uses different words
He gives scientific evidence against her claim
He draws a general rule from one example
He twists her claim into an extreme one and argues against that instead
questions.x: Sara asked for more sleep, not sleeping all day. Hamza attacks a distorted version of her point, so he never answers what she actually said.

questions.q: A sign in a hospital ward says: "Please keep your voices low; patients are resting." Which assumption does the sign make?
o: Loud voices can disturb resting patients
All patients in the ward are asleep
questions.x: Asking for quiet so that patients can rest assumes noise could disturb them. It does not claim every patient is asleep.

questions.q: Find the next letter: Y, V, S, P, ?
questions.x: Each letter moves 3 places back: Y(25), V(22), S(19), P(16), so next is M(13).

questions.q: Find the next number: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ?
questions.x: Each term is n x (n + 1): 1x2, 2x3, 3x4, 4x5, 5x6, so next is 6 x 7 = 42. The differences 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 give the same result.

questions.q: Nida is facing north-west. She turns 135 degrees clockwise. Which direction is she facing now?
questions.x: Clockwise from north-west: 45 degrees brings her to north, and another 90 degrees to east.

questions.q: Sana, Hina and Nida are a pharmacist, a dentist and a lawyer, one each. Hina is not the pharmacist. Nida is neither the dentist nor the pharmacist. Who is the pharmacist?
questions.x: Nida must be the lawyer. Hina is not the pharmacist, so she is the dentist, leaving Sana as the pharmacist.

questions.q: Statement: Many vehicles speed on the busy road outside a primary school during school hours. Courses of action: I. Speed breakers and warning signs should be placed near the school. II. Traffic police should be posted at the school's opening and closing times. III. Children should be taught how to cross the road safely. Which course(s) of action follow?
o: I, II and III all follow
questions.x: Speed breakers slow vehicles, police control traffic at the busiest times, and road-safety lessons protect the children. All three are practical.

questions.q: Statement: A shopkeeper gave one customer the wrong change by mistake and corrected it when told. Courses of action: I. His shop licence should be cancelled. II. All shops in the area should be made to use only card payments. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: One honest mistake that was quickly corrected needs no action. Cancelling his licence is extreme, and forcing card payments on every shop does not follow.

questions.q: A student believes that sleeping with a book under his pillow will help him remember what is in it. Which is a valid argument against this belief?
o: Pillows are too soft to hold books
Some books are too thick to put under a pillow
Other students also keep books under their pillows
Memory depends on studying and revising; a book under the pillow cannot pass information into the brain
questions.x: Learning comes from reading and practice. Having a book nearby while asleep gives the brain no information to store.
